cases.title: credential-guard 2.11: single-quoted prose is literal
cases.body:
Fixes the false positive I hit while landing [#86](https://github.com/sanlee-ys/agent-ops/pull/86).

## What was wrong

The v2.1 prose exemption voids itself on any `$` or backtick in the value. That is right for a **double-quoted** value, where both substitute — and wrong for a **single-quoted** one, where neither does, in POSIX shells and in PowerShell alike.

A Markdown PR body is mostly backticks, so this was refused as a credential read:

```
gh pr create --body '... `~/.claude/settings.json` ...'
```

**The block is not the damage — the workaround is.** I did not stop and ask; I switched to `--body-file` and carried on. That is the exact failure [`security/posture.md`](https://github.com/sanlee-ys/agent-ops/blob/main/security/posture.md) limit #5 predicted in writing ("a guard nobody can use gets routed around"), and it is worse than a plain nuisance here: `--body-file` genuinely reads the named file, so the guard pushed traffic *from* a shape it can analyse *to* one it must default-deny.

## The fix, and why it is narrow

Quote-aware literalness, not a looser pattern. Single quotes **only**, and only when the value is not nested inside a double-quoted region — because there it is not literal at all:

```
bash -c "gh pr create --body '$(cat ~/.env)'"
```

The outer quotes substitute before the inner single quotes are ever interpreted, so the secret is published. `_inside_double_quotes` draws that line, and anything it cannot classify falls through to the existing check. The same test now gates `PROSE_FLAG_CRED_VAR`, since `--body '$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY'` publishes the literal name, not the key.

## Verified both directions, before shipping

Per the standing decoy discipline — the measured matrix, not an argument that the code looks right:

| Must stay blocked | Result |
|---|---|
| `bash -c`, `sh -c`, `powershell -c` nesting (4 shapes) | BLOCK |
| `--body "$(cat ~/.env)"`, backtick-cat, `"$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"` | BLOCK |
| `--body-file` / `-F`, unquoted value | BLOCK |
| real reads (`cat ~/.claude/settings.json`) | BLOCK |

| Now correctly allowed | Result |
|---|---|
| single-quoted Markdown backticks | allow |
| single-quoted `$5`, literal `$(cat …)` text, literal `$VAR` | allow |
| plain prose, both quote styles (unchanged) | allow |

Suite **124 → 129 passed**; vendor adapters **79 passed, 8 subtests**.

## Also in here

Re-copies canon into `vendors/claude/plugin/hooks/`, which that plugin's README requires ("edit canon, then re-copy") and which the 2.10 change skipped — the copy was sitting at **2.9**. That is limit #6's drift class, caught only because this fix had to touch the file. The other four plugin copies were already in sync.

## Deployment note

On Windows the live hook is a regular file **copy**, so this is not active on that machine until `setup-windows.ps1` re-runs — already queued in the machine-config repo's parity file. macOS symlinks pick it up on pull. Until then the false positive persists locally, which is cosmetic: single-quoted prose keeps getting blocked, and nothing unsafe is newly allowed.

cases.title: Guard: a metadata op is safe wherever it sits; `.pub` is not a key (v2.3)
cases.body:
Fixes a confirmed false positive in the credential guard's v2 path-based
default-deny — and a self-contradicting one:

```
"ed25519: $(Test-Path $HOME\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub)"
  -> blocked, advising "use a metadata command (ls / stat / Test-Path)"
```

Two independent defects produced that contradiction.

## 1. The metadata exemption was positional

v2 classified a segment by its **leading** command. Bare `Test-Path <path>`
reached the safe allowlist; wrapped in a substitution, the leading token is a
quoted string, which is not a safe command, so the segment fell to
default-deny. A probe confirmed the split before any code changed — the bare
form already passed, so the exemption existed and was simply unreachable here.
The same shape blocked `if (Test-Path ~/.ssh/id_rsa)`.

v2.3 classifies each **nested command unit** on its own terms (`$( )`,
backticks, `<( )`, bare `( )` groups) and then judges the outer command with
those units blanked. The mere presence of `$(` is no longer disqualifying; the
substitution gets read instead.

Two properties keep the recursion from becoming a laundering hole:

| Shape | Why it still blocks |
| --- | --- |
| `cat $(echo ~/.ssh/id_rsa)` | Clearing a unit must not hide the path from a reader that **receives** it. Only a unit whose output is a bare value (`Test-Path`, `test`) stops the outer command being scrutinised; `echo`/`ls`/a bare quoted path hand the path text onward. |
| `"$(Test-Path ~/.ssh/id_rsa; cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa)"` | A unit body is a command **list** and is re-split before classifying. |

The second was **found by an adversarial pass on this fix before it shipped** —
the first draft judged that body on `Test-Path` alone and let the chained
reader ride in behind it. The top-level splitter can't catch it: it leaves
separators inside quotes alone, which is exactly where the shape lives.

A paren inside a *quoted* string stays literal text and is not treated as a
unit, so an interpreter one-liner is not torn into fragments that each look
harmless.

## 2. `.pub` matched the private-key pattern

A `.pub` file is the *public* half of a keypair — printed, pasted into GitHub,
appended to `authorized_keys` as a matter of routine. Blocking it is a pure
false positive, and the kind that teaches reaching for `MASK-OK` on a
non-secret. Unlike `.pem` (ambiguous between a cert and a key, hence the
`key`/`priv` guard on `PUBLIC_CERT`), `.pub` is unambiguous by convention, so
`deploy-key.pub` is exempt too.

The pattern now matches the whole trailing suffix so the exemption still judges
a **complete** basename: `id_rsa.pub.bak` does not qualify. That is the
anchoring discipline `PUBLIC_CERT` learned in red-team round 2 — the first
draft got this wrong and two of my own tests caught it.

## Verification

- `TestNestedMetadataFalsePositive` / `TestPublicKeyNotASecret`: the repro plus
  the nested/group/`[bool]`/`if` forms and the required metadata set allowed;
  content reads, both laundering shapes, and every private half still blocked.
- Differentially probed against the pre-change baseline, so every
  `BLOCK -> ALLOW` transition is an intended one and nothing loosened silently.
- 127 tests pass repo-wide (includes #25's `Env:` cases, rebased onto it).
- Live deploy at `~/.claude/hooks/` re-synced from canonical and smoke-tested
  against a **decoy** keypair rather than the real key, since a regression here
  would print an actual private key: private read blocked, `.pub` read allowed,
  nested `Test-Path` allowed. Decoy deleted.

Companion to #25 — same day, same file, disjoint rules. That one covered the
env-dump half of the report; this is the path half.

cases.title: feat: a PreToolUse guard against whole-tree git staging
cases.body:
Blocks `git add -A`, `git add -u`, `git add .` and `git commit -a`, with a `STAGE-ALL-OK` per-command override.

## Why a hook and not a rule

`operating-model.md` already said to stage explicit paths. On 2026-07-18/19 that rule failed **twice in a single session** — the second time *after* the first was already a known lesson in the same conversation, sweeping six files of another session's in-flight work onto a default branch.

That is what a reflex looks like from the outside, and a reflex is not fixed by writing the rule down more firmly. This repo's whole argument is that a rule without a mechanical backstop drifts silently; this is that argument applied to the repo's own operating model.

## The constraint that shaped the implementation

**The guard must not block prose.** The commit messages, PR bodies and postmortems describing these incidents quote `git add -u` verbatim — a guard that cannot document itself gets disabled rather than obeyed. `credential-guard` v1 hit this exact wall by blocking its own commit message for quoting an example.

So it strips heredoc bodies, tokenizes with `shlex` so quoted text collapses into a single token, and only counts a flag in real command position. Grepping for `-A` would have been four lines and unusable.

## Tests

25 cases, both halves:

- **Blocked:** every whole-tree shape, including `git -C <repo> add -u`, `-am`, and the offence buried in a later segment of `add && commit && push`.
- **Allowed:** explicit paths, `--amend` (long-form, contains an `a` — a sloppy matcher blocks it), `git add -p`, `git stash -u`, `git clean -A`, non-git commands, non-shell tools.
- **Prose:** four cases lifted from the actual commit messages written the day it was built — a flag inside `-m`, inside `echo`, inside a commit heredoc, inside a `gh pr create` body heredoc.
- **Fails open** on an unparseable payload; a broken hook must not wedge every tool call.

## Verified live

Wired into `settings.json` and exercised in-session — `git -C <repo> add -u` blocked with the guidance message, explicit-path staging unaffected. Provisioning for both platforms is in [REDACTED: publication boundary] (canonical stays here, same as `credential-guard`).

cases.title: config-change-guard v1.1: check what the name promised
cases.body:
## The problem

`config-change-guard.py` v1.0 checked `disableAllHooks`, plus a substring search
for four guard names over the serialized `hooks` blob. Both directions were
narrower than the name "config tamper guard" implies — and the gap was not
academic. A settings file could keep all four guard names, pass v1.0 cleanly,
and still hand the session unrestricted power.

## What v1.1 blocks that v1.0 called an intact chain

| Escalation | v1.0 | v1.1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `permissions.defaultMode: "bypassPermissions"` | allowed — `permissions` was never read | **blocked** |
| `permissions.allow: ["Bash"]` / `Bash(*)` / `Bash(:*)` / `Bash(*:*)` | allowed | **blocked** |
| `env: {ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL: …}` — model traffic redirected | allowed | **blocked** |
| guard moved to `PostToolUse` (runs after the call; cannot refuse) | allowed — name still in the blob | **blocked** |
| guard given `"matcher": ""` (matches nothing) | allowed | **blocked** |
| command repointed at `credential-guard-disabled.py` | allowed — that string *contains* `credential-guard` | **blocked** |

The first three are new checks. The last three fall out of replacing the
substring search with a **structural** one: each guard must appear under its
expected event, with a non-empty matcher, and a command naming the exact
`<guard>.py` file. Every check is additive — nothing v1.0 refused is now allowed.

## The usability half is the load-bearing half

This guard sits on the one file a false positive cannot be repaired from: a
wrong block bricks the config, and the repair is itself a config change the
guard blocks again. So every new check fires only on an unambiguously dangerous
value, never a merely unusual one. Pinned as **allowed**, beside the escalations:

- prefixed allow rules — `Bash(git status)`, `Bash(gh pr view *)`, `Bash(rm -rf:*)`
  — ordinary allowlist maintenance, and narrowing those is `/doctor`'s job
- a benign `env` block (`EDITOR`, `TZ`, …); an `env` block per se is normal
- `plan` / `acceptEdits` / `default` / `auto` — user preferences, not tampering
- an **absent** `matcher` key, which means "all tools" in Claude Code — only an
  explicitly empty matcher is the neutering shape
- bare non-shell tool names (`Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `Agent`)
- a missing or malformed `permissions` key, and junk in the `hooks` tree

## Verification

- `tests/test_config_change_guard.py`: **22 → 36 cases, all green.**
- Full repo suite: **440/440 green** (`python -m unittest discover -s tests`).
- Both copies `py_compile` clean; `scripts/githooks/pre-commit` (redline guard) exit 0.
- **The false-block case that actually matters:** fed a `user_settings`
  `ConfigChange` payload pointing at the real canonical `settings.json` that
  provisions these machines → **ALLOWED** (empty stdout, exit 0).

## Still UNMEASURED — unchanged by this PR, and stated plainly

Whether `ConfigChange` fires when a *tool* edits a settings file, and whether
`{"decision": "block"}` actually vetoes the change, remain unobserved. A third
attempt to measure closed off today: standing up a scratch probe rig (headless
child session + `--settings` wiring a log-only probe) was refused by
`credential-guard` at the *parent* session, because composing the command
requires naming a Claude config path. **That block was correct and was not
worked around**; the probe log was confirmed never created, so no data exists.

`hooks/README.md` now carries all three closures. Per `security/posture.md`
limit 7 an unmeasured claim does not count — so a green suite here means "would
refuse the right things if it ran", not "is enforcing anything".

## Notes

- `vendors/claude/plugin/hooks/config-change-guard.py` is a derived copy;
  re-copied from canon per that README's edit-canon-then-re-copy rule, and
  verified byte-identical.
- Canonical home was already settled at `hooks/config-change-guard.py` by
  ADR-013 + the `sync-claude-hooks` registry ([REDACTED: publication boundary] #106); this PR conforms to
  it rather than proposing anywhere new.

cases.title: scripts: check HANDOFF.md against git and the forge
cases.body:
## What this adds

A check for a class of drift that nothing catches today. A HANDOFF State
section restates facts that `git` and the forge hold exactly: the open pull
requests, the newest tag, the top CHANGELOG entry, the branch. The merged set
moves past the prose the same day, and nothing turns red when it does.

- `scripts/handoff_check.py` reads a repo's HANDOFF.md, derives the same facts,
  and prints each claim as MATCH, DRIFT, or UNMEASURED. Six checks. Stdlib
  only.
- `tests/test_handoff_check.py`, 63 tests. Recorded `git` and `gh` output
  through a fake `run`, so the suite needs no network, no forge, and no repo.
- `conventions/handoff-check.md` records the decision, the three rules the
  report rests on, six honest limits, and both runs from 2026-09-20.
- One README row for the convention and one for the script, plus the scripts
  index and the CLAUDE.md conventions list.

## Why a check, not a generator

Two build paths were open. Generate the State section from `gh` and the
CHANGELOG, or read it and report what disagrees. This takes the second.

A generated State section carries only the facts the generator knows. The
judgement around them is the part that helps the next session: which pull
request matters, what a number means, what to do first. A generator deletes
that prose or leaves it beside a machine block that nobody trusts. A check
leaves the writer in charge and refuses to let one class of claim go quiet.

The tool never edits HANDOFF.md. `TestNeverWrites` compares the file bytes
before and after a full run.

## Three rules the report rests on

- **Absent is not zero.** A `gh` call that fails reports UNMEASURED with the
  reason, never an empty set of open pull requests. A missing HANDOFF.md exits
  2, because a deleted file must not report the same green as a correct one.
- **The remote is the authority.** Branches and tags come from `git ls-remote`,
  never from a remote-tracking ref, which is a local cache that can carry the
  stale claim the check exists to catch. `reconcile.py` made the same call.
- **A false DRIFT is the expensive error.** A check that reports a drift which
  is not there trains the reader to skip the output. Every detector
  under-reports rather than guesses, and the convention page states where.

## Measured against the motivating case

`defense-news-classifier`, HANDOFF dated 2026-08-02. Exit code 1, five DRIFT
rows and one UNMEASURED. The row that produced this work:

```
DRIFT      job-consistency  (handoff)
    claimed  Owner-only pending: Running the higher-power re-run (job 3)
    derived  job 3 DONE in Next jobs: The higher-power re-run
    one piece of work carries two answers in one file. Shared words: higher, power
```

That check keys on the job's own words, never on the job number. A finished job
legitimately hands one remaining step to the owner, and that step cites the job
it came from. Job 1 in the same file does exactly that, and the check stays
quiet on it. Both cases are pinned by tests.

A run against a real file also found a silent defect that review had missed: a
dependency bump written as `4.37.3` was reading as the newest release of the
repo, which is usually the highest number on the page. The tag check reported a
false MATCH and the drift stayed. A version in prose now needs the leading `v`.

The classifier repo was read-only in this lane. Nothing here edits its HANDOFF.

## Verification

- `python -m unittest discover -s tests -p "test_*.py"`: green.
- Both runs in the convention page are real output from this branch, with
  local paths shown `~`-style per the publication boundary.

cases.title: Guard: `Env:` PSDrive is a dump, `$env:NAME` in a path is not (v2.2)
cases.body:
## The false positive

This benign command was blocked with the env-dump message:

```
Get-ChildItem "$env:USERPROFILE\.ssh" -Filter *.pub -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Name
```

The rule was `\bGet-ChildItem\b[^|]*\bEnv:` — **any** `Get-ChildItem` followed
anywhere in the segment by the text `Env:`. But PowerShell spells two different
things `env:`:

| Form | What it is | Should be |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Get-ChildItem Env:` | the **Env: PSDrive** enumerated as a path argument — every variable, values included | blocked (dump) |
| `Get-ChildItem "$env:USERPROFILE\.ssh"` | a **variable dereference** used to build a path; lists a directory, touches no value | allowed |
| `Get-ChildItem Env:GITHUB_TOKEN` | one **named** variable printed — not a dump, still a credential print | blocked (targeted read) |
| `Get-ChildItem Env:PATH` | one named non-credential variable | allowed |

Only the first row is an environment dump. Rows 2 and 4 were being blocked.

## The fix

Anchor **both ends** of the token, so `Env:` only matches as the PSDrive root in
the path-argument position:

- it must **follow** whitespace (after the cmdlet and any `-Flag`s), optionally
  quoted, and never a `$` — that alone kills `"$env:USERPROFILE\.ssh"`, and it's
  why the sibling `(dir|ls|gci)\s+env:` alternatives never had this bug (they
  already required the whitespace). They fold into the one rule now.
- it must **end** there, bar a `\`/`/` root separator and a `*` wildcard — so
  `Env:PATH` is a targeted read rather than a dump.

## The half of this fix that isn't the fix

Narrowing "dump" to the bare drive root moves `Env:NAME` out of the dump rule —
and the over-broad rule had been *incidentally* catching real credential reads
through it (`Get-ChildItem Env:GITHUB_TOKEN`, `ls Env:GH_TOKEN`, `dir
Env:GH_TOKEN` were all blocked only because of the very breadth being removed).
So `CRED_VAR_READ` is widened to the listing cmdlets alongside the
`Get-Item`/`Get-Content` forms it already had.

Without that second edit this PR would have shipped a hole while removing a
false positive. That's the general shape worth remembering: **a tightening has
to be checked for the true positives it was catching by accident.**

## Regression cases, both directions

`TestEnvDriveFalsePositive`, following the suite's existing discipline of
pinning a blocked case *and* an allowed case per change:

- **must allow** (8): the exact repro, `Get-ChildItem "$env:USERPROFILE\.ssh"`,
  `Get-ChildItem $env:TEMP`, `Test-Path $env:APPDATA\foo`, `gci
  $env:LOCALAPPDATA`, `-Path "$env:ProgramData\logs"`, …
- **must block** (11): `Get-ChildItem Env:`, `gci env:`, `ls Env:\`,
  `Get-ChildItem -Path Env:`, `Get-ChildItem "Env:"`, `Env:\*`, `dir env:`,
  `Get-Item Env:*`, `(Get-ChildItem Env:).Count`, `-Force Env:`, piped form
- **must still block** (5): targeted credential reads via the listing cmdlets
- **must still allow**: `Env:PATH` via both `Get-Item` and `Get-ChildItem`

## Bash-side audit

Checked whether the same class exists for `env` / `printenv` / `set` /
`declare -p` — i.e. whether a path or argument containing the literal word `env`
can trip them. **It can't:** those rules are whole-segment anchored
(`^\s*env\s*$`) or flag-bearing (`declare\s+-\w*p`), so `.venv/`, `env/`,
`--env-file`, `python -m venv env`, `/usr/bin/env`, `conda env list` and
`docker run --env` never matched. Verified empirically against the guard, and
pinned as tests so a future widening of those rules has to fail a test on
purpose rather than silently reintroduce this class.

## Notes

- `hook-version` 2.1 → 2.2 (same v2 architecture, corrected behaviour), so every
  deployed copy is stale until re-synced — per `security/README.md`.
- Full suite green: 120 tests.
- One adjacent finding left alone deliberately: `Get-Variable PATH` (positional
  name, no `-Name` flag) is blocked by `\bGet-Variable\b(?![^|]*-Name)`, which is
  arguably the same "can't tell a dump from a targeted read" shape. Unlike
  `Env:`, narrowing it would open a real gap — the `Variable:` drive holds shell
  variables the name-based `CRED_VAR_READ` can't screen (`$k = $env:SECRET;
  Get-Variable k`). That's a posture call, not a bug fix, so it's filed
  separately rather than decided here.

cases.title: Guard the invariant: published commits don't get dropped from main
cases.body:
## What happened

On 2026-07-26 two sessions worked one direct-to-main repo in the same clone. Session B reset past a commit Session A had already pushed, recommitted its own work, and force-pushed over the top. Session A's commit was recovered only because it was still in the reflog. Nothing announced the loss — it surfaced when a later edit could not find its own text.

## What the permission layer actually did

Checked before designing anything, because if the `ask` rules simply failed, the fix would be to repair them and stop. They did not simply fail:

1. **The reset was correctly allowed.** `git -C <repo> reset --soft de133f2` returned in 2.2s — no human read a prompt. Nor should one have: a soft reset destroys nothing locally, the operative gate is the auto-mode classifier (which denies resets under `[Irreversible Local Destruction]`), and the session had tagged a backup first.
2. **The force-push was not covered.** The `ask` list carried `--force` and `-f` in four shapes each, and **no** entry for `--force-with-lease`, so it fell through to the `git push` allow rule. A real gap — closed in the companion [REDACTED: publication boundary] PR.
3. **The lease protected nothing.** It compares the remote-*tracking* ref, and a background fetch had refreshed it, so the lease passed.

**The finding that drove the design:** closing gap 2 alone would not have prevented this, because finding 1 stands. The reset was the *safe* verb. The dangerous fact — *the range you are discarding holds a commit you did not write, and it is already on the remote* — is in the repository, not the command string, so no prefix rule and no classifier reading the command can reach it.

## The guard

`hooks/published-history-guard.py` — a stateful `PreToolUse` hook that asks git, at the moment of the call, what the command would actually destroy. Blocks a history-rewriting push or a backward `reset` on `main` **only when** published commits sit in the discarded range.

- **Both shapes, and the reset is the real fix** — it would have fired 49 seconds before the destructive push, before the session built two more commits on a doomed base.
- **`ls-remote`, never the tracking ref** — the tracking ref is what defeated `--force-with-lease`.
- **`main` only** — guarding feature branches would fire constantly for no risk, and a guard that cries wolf gets routed around.
- **Fails open, with one stated exception**: having identified a rewrite of `main`, it blocks if it *cannot verify* what would be destroyed.
- Override `REWRITE-MAIN-OK`, per-command, for deliberate rewrites like the de-identification squash.

## Options weighed (ADR-007)

- **(a) `pre-push` git hook** — fires three minutes too late, no propagation path for `pre-push` across the fleet. Worth revisiting as defence-in-depth.
- **(b) Server-side branch protection — DISQUALIFIED, not rejected.** Rulesets and branch protection are **paid features for private repos**; the API returns `403 Upgrade to GitHub Pro`. Available on exactly the repos that already have a PR gate, unavailable on the private direct-to-main ones that need it. Also a poor fit for legitimate rewrites, which would require toggling protection off and back on.
- **(c) A written rule alone** — necessary but insufficient; `git-staging-guard.py` exists because a behavioural rule failed twice in two days.

## Verification

26 new checks against **real** repositories (a bare remote plus clones playing Session A and Session B), suite green at 166. Verified by mutation, not just by passing:

| Mutation | Checks that fail |
|---|---|
| Both checks neutered | 10 |
| `_remote_head` regressed to the tracking ref | 7 |

Two defects surfaced by running it against the reconstruction, both of which made it fail **open** on the shape it exists to catch:

- posix-mode `shlex` ate backslashes, mangling Windows `-C` paths so the repo never resolved;
- a clone that hadn't fetched since the remote moved answered every ancestry question "unknown" — the *normal* state for the session being guarded.

Neither was visible by reading the code.

## Also here

- `conventions/parallel-sessions.md` gains the divergence-recovery rule: **rebase onto `main`, never reset back to where you started.** The compressed shared block is deliberately left alone — editing it drifts every public consumer at once and reddens the drift check until each is swept, which is separate work.
- README entry and a CI syntax-check line.

cases.title: feat: a PreToolUse guard against whole-tree git staging
cases.body:
Blocks `git add -A`, `git add -u`, `git add .` and `git commit -a`, with a `STAGE-ALL-OK` per-command override.

## Why a hook and not a rule

`operating-model.md` already said to stage explicit paths. On 2026-07-18/19 that rule failed **twice in a single session** — the second time *after* the first was already a known lesson in the same conversation, sweeping six files of another session's in-flight work onto a default branch.

That is what a reflex looks like from the outside, and a reflex is not fixed by writing the rule down more firmly. This repo's whole argument is that a rule without a mechanical backstop drifts silently; this is that argument applied to the repo's own operating model.

## The constraint that shaped the implementation

**The guard must not block prose.** The commit messages, PR bodies and postmortems describing these incidents quote `git add -u` verbatim — a guard that cannot document itself gets disabled rather than obeyed. `credential-guard` v1 hit this exact wall by blocking its own commit message for quoting an example.

So it strips heredoc bodies, tokenizes with `shlex` so quoted text collapses into a single token, and only counts a flag in real command position. Grepping for `-A` would have been four lines and unusable.

## Tests

25 cases, both halves:

- **Blocked:** every whole-tree shape, including `git -C <repo> add -u`, `-am`, and the offence buried in a later segment of `add && commit && push`.
- **Allowed:** explicit paths, `--amend` (long-form, contains an `a` — a sloppy matcher blocks it), `git add -p`, `git stash -u`, `git clean -A`, non-git commands, non-shell tools.
- **Prose:** four cases lifted from the actual commit messages written the day it was built — a flag inside `-m`, inside `echo`, inside a commit heredoc, inside a `gh pr create` body heredoc.
- **Fails open** on an unparseable payload; a broken hook must not wedge every tool call.

## Verified live

Wired into `settings.json` and exercised in-session — `git -C <repo> add -u` blocked with the guidance message, explicit-path staging unaffected. Provisioning for both platforms is in [REDACTED: publication boundary] (canonical stays here, same as `credential-guard`).

cases.title: feat(guards): blast × reversibility scoring, redact-and-allow, exit-2 backstop (ADR-015)
cases.body:
Ports three designs from the public secguard project (Apache-2.0 + Commons Clause) into the guard chain. The designs are ported; the code is original Python. Design record: `decisions/ADR-015-blast-reversibility-scoring-and-redaction.md`.

## What this adds

1. **`hooks/destructive-command-guard.py`** — blast × reversibility scoring for locally destructive commands. Each rule id declares `(blast 0-4, reversibility 0-4)`; `risk = blast + (4 - reversibility)` buckets into allow / warn / confirm / block. The headline split: `git reset --soft` scores (0, 4) and passes; `git reset --hard` scores (1, 0) and asks. This closes the local-destruction half of the 2026-07-26 classifier gap (ADR-007 covers the published-history half and is not duplicated). Overrides: `RISK-OK` per command; `guard-scoring.json` per rule, per cell, or per score.
2. **exit(2) backstop** — a block-bucket verdict prints the deny JSON, writes the reason to stderr, and exits 2, which the harness honours even in `bypassPermissions` mode. The three existing redline guards already did this; ADR-015 records it as policy.
3. **`security/secret-redaction-guard.py`** — redact-and-allow for secret VALUES. It recursively walks `tool_input`, replaces each match with `[REDACTED:<rule_id>]`, and returns allow with `hookSpecificOutput.updatedInput` plus a reason naming the count and types. The codex target denies instead (its contract cannot rewrite input and ignores `ask`).

Both guards carry a shadow mode (`AGENT_OPS_GUARD_SHADOW` logs `would <action>` and enforces nothing) and asymmetric fail-open (an unparseable segment allows unless it names a destructive trigger keyword; then it escalates to confirm).

## Verification

- 57 new tests drive both guards with real PreToolUse JSON payloads on stdin; full suite green at 610 (`python -m unittest discover -s tests`).
- Pinned: the 25-cell matrix snapshot, both monotonicity invariants, the soft/hard reset split, override token, shadow truthy/falsy values, all three config override layers plus the bad-config path, redaction idempotency, the codex deny path, and clean-prose negatives.
- Not verified: neither guard is wired on a live machine. The machine-config deploy step must add both files before anything enforces. Live-harness acceptance of `updatedInput` is a doc claim until measured (stated in ADR-015).

cases.title: Build the generic stale-generated-file CI gate (ADR-003 backlog item)
cases.body:
The named ADR-003 backlog item, built: a reusable CI gate for repos that commit
build output next to its source. Rebuild from source, `git diff` the declared
outputs, fail on drift. Generalizes learning-notes' repo-local `generated-files`
job — deterministic, no judgment calls, no model in the loop.

Per-repo variables (build commands, watched paths) live in the consumer's
`.generated-drift.toml`; consumers wire one job against the `workflow_call`
wrapper. Exit codes are the interface and are deliberately distinct: `0` clean,
`1` drift (rebuild and commit), `2` operator/config error. That split matters —
a watched path already dirty before any build ran makes drift unattributable,
so it fails as operator error rather than pretending to be a drift finding.

Orthogonal to `shared-block-drift.yml` already on `main`: that one checks this
repo's own convention blocks against their mirrors; this one checks any
consumer repo's build output against its source.

Recovered from the abandoned `claude/in-flight-items-xuoe93` branch (original
commit `2d6f61e`, 2026-07-10) during the weekly hygiene sweep. Cherry-picked
onto current `main` rather than merged — the branch was ~25 commits behind and
carried a second unrelated concern, which landed separately in #48. Two
conflicts resolved by hand, both additive: `CLAUDE.md` and `scripts/README.md`
had each grown a new section on `main` since, so both sides are kept.

**Verification:** `tests/test_generated_drift.py` 8/8 pass and the full suite
exits 0 locally; `sync-shared-blocks.py --check` reports all blocks in sync,
confirming the `CLAUDE.md` resolution landed outside the marker regions.

cases.title: Guard: naming one variable is a read, not a dump (v2.4)
cases.body:
Follow-up to #25, which fixed the `Env:` PSDrive false positive and left this
one filed rather than decided, on the grounds that narrowing it was a posture
call rather than a mechanical fix. This decides it.

## What the rule actually did

The v2 rule was `\bGet-Variable\b(?![^|]*-Name)` — *"no `-Name` anywhere in the
segment, so it must be a dump."* Measured against real commands rather than read
off the regex, it was wrong in **three directions at once**:

| Command | v2 | Correct |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Get-Variable PATH` | blocked | allow — names one variable, positionally |
| `git checkout -b fix/get-variable-fp` | blocked | allow — it's a branch name |
| `rg 'Get-Variable' security/` | blocked | allow — you couldn't grep for the rule's own name |
| `Get-Variable -Name *` | **allowed** | block — `-Name` was an unconditional escape hatch, so a wildcard dump walked straight through it |
| `gv` | **allowed** | block — the alias was never named |

Rows 2 and 3 are the same root cause as the `Env:` bug in #25: matching literal
text *anywhere* in the segment instead of in a command position. This one
announced itself — the guard blocked the `git worktree add -b
fix/get-variable-targeted-read` that was creating the branch to fix it.

## The posture question, and why it resolves cleanly

The concern on file was that narrowing row 1 loses protection the name-based
`CRED_VAR_READ` screen can't replace:

```powershell
$k = $env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY   # secret is now in a variable called `k`
Get-Variable k                # ...and `k` looks nothing like a credential
```

Blocking every unnamed `Get-Variable` did catch that. **But it was never buying
the protection it appeared to** — `Get-Variable -Name k`, the same read more
idiomatically spelled, was already allowed. The rule caught laundering only when
the caller happened to use positional syntax, which is a coin flip, not a
control. Verified both ways before deciding.

So: narrow. Variable laundering *is* copy-then-read laundering (`cp secret x;
cat x`) one container down, and that's already explicitly out of scope for
exactly this reason — the threat model is non-adversarial agent mistakes, and an
agent that assigns a secret to `$k` and prints `$k` isn't the failure this hook
exists to stop. This makes an existing boundary consistent rather than moving
it. It's now listed with the other bounded-out shapes in the README and asserted
as **allowed** in `TestBoundedOutOfScope`, following the suite's convention that
a deliberate non-block is a test so a well-meaning future "fix" fails on
purpose.

Because rows 4 and 5 close at the same time, this removes two false positives
**and** two real gaps. It isn't a safety-for-convenience trade.

## Implementation

The rule is now the natural one: **a dump is an invocation that names no
specific variable, or names a wildcard.** That's a token walk
(`_get_variable_is_dump`) rather than a lookahead, so `-Scope Global` (a flag
consuming its value) and `-ValueOnly PATH` (a switch plus a name) are read
correctly — a regex can't distinguish those without enumerating the flag table
anyway, and the walk makes the intent legible.

`Variable:` also gets the drive-root treatment `Env:` got in v2.2; they share
`_PS_DRIVE_DUMP` now. `Get-ChildItem Variable:` blocks (it didn't before — only
`dir`/`ls` were named), `ls Variable:PATH` is a targeted read, and
`ls Variable:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` still blocks on the credential-name screen —
the same guard rail the `Env:` tightening needed.

## Tests

`TestGetVariableTargetedRead`, both directions, plus a class asserting the v2.2
`Env:` contract is untouched by the `_PS_ENV_DRIVE` → `_PS_DRIVE_DUMP`
generalisation. 133 tests, green.

## Version

**2.4.** v2.3 (#26) landed while this was in review, so this has been rebased on
top of it and the numbering is contiguous: 2.2 -> 2.3 -> 2.4. The two changes
touch different functions; the only textual conflicts were the version header,
the README section list, and adjacent test classes, all resolved by keeping both
sides. Full suite green at 133 tests with both changes in, and the v2.2 `Env:`
contract is re-asserted under `test_env_drive_behaviour_unchanged_by_the_generalisation`
since `_PS_ENV_DRIVE` became `_PS_DRIVE_DUMP` here.

cases.title: Guard: an anchored dump rule needs a segment to anchor to (v2.5)
cases.body:
`env` was blocked. `echo $(env)` was not — and it runs the same full dump. Also
allowed: `"$(env)"`, `echo $(printenv)`, `x=$(env)`, ``echo `env` ``.

Pre-existing gap: older than #25 and #26, confirmed on the pre-v2.2 baseline.
Filed from the #26 session as a background task rather than folded into it.

## The cause is not a rule that is too narrow

The bare-dump alternatives are anchored to a whole segment (`^\s*env\s*$`,
`^\s*printenv\s*$`, `^\s*set\s*$`), and that anchoring is **load-bearing** — it
is the only reason `.venv/bin`, `--env-file`, `conda env list`, `/usr/bin/env`
and `env -u VAR cmd` don't match (pinned since #25). Loosening it would trade
this gap for that entire family of false positives.

The cause is that `main()` only ever handed those rules the **top-level**
segment, so a dump one container down never got the anchor's attention. A
substitution body is a command in its own right, so it is now offered to them as
a segment — recursively, and re-split first, because a body is a command *list*.
This reuses the unit machinery #26 added.

## Two narrower calls inside that

- **Only the env-dump rule gets the extra pass.** `CRED_VAR_READ` and
  `MCP_GET_PATTERN` are un-anchored, so their search already sees inside a
  substitution. Running `CRED_VAR_READ` per unit would *newly break*
  `[bool]($env:API_KEY)` — its standalone-statement alternatives describe a
  statement that emits a value, and a unit body's value is consumed by the
  expression around it. The parenthesised spelling of the guard's own
  recommended existence check must not become a block. (My chip proposed running
  all three; that turned out to be wrong.)
- **The `git commit -m` prose skip does not extend to unit bodies.** It exempts
  a *message*; a substitution body is executed code whatever encloses it. So
  `git commit -m "document $(env) in the runbook"` blocks — double quotes run it
  — while the single-quoted spelling stays allowed.

## Half the fix is in the splitter

`_split_segments` cut on `;`/`|`/`&` without regard for parens, so
`echo $(cd /tmp; env)` arrived as `echo $(cd /tmp` and `env)` — and
`^\s*env\s*$` cannot match `env)`. **A fragment defeats an anchored rule as
thoroughly as never being shown the text.**

Segments now hold parentheses together. Nested units are re-split from their
bodies anyway, so no coverage is lost. An unbalanced `(` stops splitting for the
rest of the command — safe rather than blinding, since the trailing text still
lands in a unit body (`_balanced` runs an unterminated group to end of segment)
and both callers re-split it. I attacked that directly: `echo ( ; cat ~/.env`,
`echo ( ; env`, `echo ( | cat …`, a stray `)`, and a quoted
`echo "(" ; cat ~/.env` all block.

## Adjacent surfaces

The chip asked whether `_GIT_ALIAS_EXEC` and the `| xargs` pre-check share the
nesting gap. They don't — both search un-anchored, so
`echo $(git -c alias.x='!printenv KEY' x)` and `echo $(echo ~/.env | xargs cat)`
were already caught. Pinned rather than assumed.

## Verification

- `TestNestedEnvDump`, both directions: ten nested dump forms blocked, the
  whole-word false-positive set still allowed, the `[bool]` casts still allowed,
  prose-vs-executed distinguished, and the splitter attacked.
- Differentially probed against `main`, so every `ALLOW → BLOCK` transition is an
  intended one and nothing newly false-positives.
- 133 tests pass.
- Live deploy re-synced and smoke-tested through the real hook: `echo $(env)`
  blocked; `env -u UV_ENV_FILE uv run …`, `echo $(ls …)` and
  `[bool]($env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY)` all still pass.

## Version number

This is **2.5, not 2.4** — #27 has 2.4 in flight. The header is a drift
tripwire, so two files must never claim the same number; a skipped minor is
cosmetic, a duplicated one defeats the mechanism. Same rule #27 applied when it
skipped my 2.3.

Note for whoever merges second: #27 is cut from before #26, so it and this
branch will collide on the header block and the README section order. The code
changes are disjoint.

cases.title: config-change-guard v1.1: check what the name promised
cases.body:
## The problem

`config-change-guard.py` v1.0 checked `disableAllHooks`, plus a substring search
for four guard names over the serialized `hooks` blob. Both directions were
narrower than the name "config tamper guard" implies — and the gap was not
academic. A settings file could keep all four guard names, pass v1.0 cleanly,
and still hand the session unrestricted power.

## What v1.1 blocks that v1.0 called an intact chain

| Escalation | v1.0 | v1.1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `permissions.defaultMode: "bypassPermissions"` | allowed — `permissions` was never read | **blocked** |
| `permissions.allow: ["Bash"]` / `Bash(*)` / `Bash(:*)` / `Bash(*:*)` | allowed | **blocked** |
| `env: {ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL: …}` — model traffic redirected | allowed | **blocked** |
| guard moved to `PostToolUse` (runs after the call; cannot refuse) | allowed — name still in the blob | **blocked** |
| guard given `"matcher": ""` (matches nothing) | allowed | **blocked** |
| command repointed at `credential-guard-disabled.py` | allowed — that string *contains* `credential-guard` | **blocked** |

The first three are new checks. The last three fall out of replacing the
substring search with a **structural** one: each guard must appear under its
expected event, with a non-empty matcher, and a command naming the exact
`<guard>.py` file. Every check is additive — nothing v1.0 refused is now allowed.

## The usability half is the load-bearing half

This guard sits on the one file a false positive cannot be repaired from: a
wrong block bricks the config, and the repair is itself a config change the
guard blocks again. So every new check fires only on an unambiguously dangerous
value, never a merely unusual one. Pinned as **allowed**, beside the escalations:

- prefixed allow rules — `Bash(git status)`, `Bash(gh pr view *)`, `Bash(rm -rf:*)`
  — ordinary allowlist maintenance, and narrowing those is `/doctor`'s job
- a benign `env` block (`EDITOR`, `TZ`, …); an `env` block per se is normal
- `plan` / `acceptEdits` / `default` / `auto` — user preferences, not tampering
- an **absent** `matcher` key, which means "all tools" in Claude Code — only an
  explicitly empty matcher is the neutering shape
- bare non-shell tool names (`Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `Agent`)
- a missing or malformed `permissions` key, and junk in the `hooks` tree

## Verification

- `tests/test_config_change_guard.py`: **22 → 36 cases, all green.**
- Full repo suite: **440/440 green** (`python -m unittest discover -s tests`).
- Both copies `py_compile` clean; `scripts/githooks/pre-commit` (redline guard) exit 0.
- **The false-block case that actually matters:** fed a `user_settings`
  `ConfigChange` payload pointing at the real canonical `settings.json` that
  provisions these machines → **ALLOWED** (empty stdout, exit 0).

## Still UNMEASURED — unchanged by this PR, and stated plainly

Whether `ConfigChange` fires when a *tool* edits a settings file, and whether
`{"decision": "block"}` actually vetoes the change, remain unobserved. A third
attempt to measure closed off today: standing up a scratch probe rig (headless
child session + `--settings` wiring a log-only probe) was refused by
`credential-guard` at the *parent* session, because composing the command
requires naming a Claude config path. **That block was correct and was not
worked around**; the probe log was confirmed never created, so no data exists.

`hooks/README.md` now carries all three closures. Per `security/posture.md`
limit 7 an unmeasured claim does not count — so a green suite here means "would
refuse the right things if it ran", not "is enforcing anything".

## Notes

- `vendors/claude/plugin/hooks/config-change-guard.py` is a derived copy;
  re-copied from canon per that README's edit-canon-then-re-copy rule, and
  verified byte-identical.
- Canonical home was already settled at `hooks/config-change-guard.py` by
  ADR-013 + the `sync-claude-hooks` registry ([REDACTED: publication boundary] #106); this PR conforms to
  it rather than proposing anywhere new.

cases.title: feat(guards): blast × reversibility scoring, redact-and-allow, exit-2 backstop (ADR-015)
cases.body:
Ports three designs from the public secguard project (Apache-2.0 + Commons Clause) into the guard chain. The designs are ported; the code is original Python. Design record: `decisions/ADR-015-blast-reversibility-scoring-and-redaction.md`.

## What this adds

1. **`hooks/destructive-command-guard.py`** — blast × reversibility scoring for locally destructive commands. Each rule id declares `(blast 0-4, reversibility 0-4)`; `risk = blast + (4 - reversibility)` buckets into allow / warn / confirm / block. The headline split: `git reset --soft` scores (0, 4) and passes; `git reset --hard` scores (1, 0) and asks. This closes the local-destruction half of the 2026-07-26 classifier gap (ADR-007 covers the published-history half and is not duplicated). Overrides: `RISK-OK` per command; `guard-scoring.json` per rule, per cell, or per score.
2. **exit(2) backstop** — a block-bucket verdict prints the deny JSON, writes the reason to stderr, and exits 2, which the harness honours even in `bypassPermissions` mode. The three existing redline guards already did this; ADR-015 records it as policy.
3. **`security/secret-redaction-guard.py`** — redact-and-allow for secret VALUES. It recursively walks `tool_input`, replaces each match with `[REDACTED:<rule_id>]`, and returns allow with `hookSpecificOutput.updatedInput` plus a reason naming the count and types. The codex target denies instead (its contract cannot rewrite input and ignores `ask`).

Both guards carry a shadow mode (`AGENT_OPS_GUARD_SHADOW` logs `would <action>` and enforces nothing) and asymmetric fail-open (an unparseable segment allows unless it names a destructive trigger keyword; then it escalates to confirm).

## Verification

- 57 new tests drive both guards with real PreToolUse JSON payloads on stdin; full suite green at 610 (`python -m unittest discover -s tests`).
- Pinned: the 25-cell matrix snapshot, both monotonicity invariants, the soft/hard reset split, override token, shadow truthy/falsy values, all three config override layers plus the bad-config path, redaction idempotency, the codex deny path, and clean-prose negatives.
- Not verified: neither guard is wired on a live machine. The machine-config deploy step must add both files before anything enforces. Live-harness acceptance of `updatedInput` is a doc claim until measured (stated in ADR-015).
